data.title: Strategy stock (MSTR) falls as MSCI index exclusion threatens passive investments
data.description:
Strategy (formerly known as MicroStrategy) stock (MSTR) fell on Friday as investors assessed the potential removal of the Bitcoin treasury company from MSCI's global equity indexes, despite a rise in Bitcoin prices.

The company also announced plans to maintain a 12% annualised dividend rate on its STRC preferred stock for November, subject to shareholder approval and related amendments taking effect.

Strategy shares declined 6% on Friday, while Bitcoin traded around $82,290, having gained more than 1.3% over the previous 24 hours.

Strategy, led by Michael Saylor, is the world's largest corporate Bitcoin holder, with 848,250 BTC.

The stock's decline highlights how factors beyond cryptocurrency prices, including index inclusion and financing costs, can influence investor sentiment towards the company.

MSCI rules put Strategy's index inclusion at risk

MSCI said on Thursday that non-operating companies would be ineligible for its Global Investable Market Indexes from the close of November 30.

The index provider plans to publish the final list of affected companies on November 11.

Strategy and Japan's Metaplanet are among the companies potentially facing removal.

SharpLink and several other cryptocurrency treasury companies are on a watchlist for possible exclusion.

The policy follows a review that MSCI began last year into whether digital asset treasury companies resemble investment funds, which are already excluded from its indexes.

MSCI deferred its original proposal in January before broadening the review to cover non-operating companies more generally.

The potential exclusion matters because passive funds tracking MSCI benchmarks are required to hold constituent stocks.

Strategy previously warned that removal could lead to $2.8 billion worth of its shares being liquidated.

Strategy has disputed MSCI's proposed classification. In a statement on Friday, the company said, “We believe the proposal is misguided.”

Strategy also argued that MSCI's distinction between operating and non-operating companies was undefined and lacked a basis in US GAAP, IFRS or recognised legal frameworks.

The company said funds tracking MSCI's Global Investable Market Indexes held just 3.1% of its outstanding shares, potentially limiting the direct impact of an exclusion.

Strategy maintains 12% STRC dividend rate

Separately, Strategy's board declared daily cash dividends on its STRC preferred stock for each calendar day in November, subject to shareholder approval and the effectiveness of related amendments.

The annualised dividend rate will remain at 12%.

Strategy said management would continue recommending that rate until STRC demonstrates “sustained, healthy trading near $100 per share.”

Payments are scheduled to begin on November 2, with each dividend payable on the business day following its record date, according to a regulatory filing.

STRC is one of Strategy's key fundraising instruments for Bitcoin purchases.

Daily dividend payments could help make the preferred stock more attractive to investors and support trading around its $100 par value.

STRC was down 0.2% at $99.33.

Bitcoin purchases and financing strategy in focus

Strategy added 250 Bitcoin for $21.5 million last week, bringing its total holdings to 848,250 BTC.

During the week ending October 4, the company repurchased $176 million worth of STRC, spending more than six times as much on the buybacks as on its $28 million in Bitcoin purchases.

The company introduced a capital framework on June 29 that allows it to sell Bitcoin to fund dividend payments.

It also raised STRC's annual dividend rate to 12% at the time.

Strategy's business model relies on raising capital through stock and debt sales to acquire Bitcoin.

While that approach has made the company a major proxy for cryptocurrency exposure in equity markets, its shares remain sensitive to financing conditions and index-related developments.

Index-related risks like MSCI’s proposed exclusion are closely watched by traders who follow stock reactions through top online trading platforms.

data.title: Jordan is driving Nike's resale volume growth: buy NKE stock?
data.description:
Nike’s (NKE) Jordan brand is gaining ground among sneaker resellers, offering an “encouraging” signal for a business still struggling to regain its footing.

Citi’s tracking showed Nike captured 72.3% of resale volume in September, a 63bps increase from August, with Jordan driving most of the improvement.

That also exceeded the 70.8% average recorded between June and August.

Still, investors should resist treating stronger resale share as proof of a financial recovery. For NKE stock, these latest figures support cautious optimism about brand appeal rather than an immediate buying case.

What Jordan’s resale volume means for Nike stock

The most important distinction is between resale market share and actual sales growth.

Nike could capture a larger portion of secondary-market transactions even if the overall market contracts.

Citi’s reported figures alone therefore cannot establish whether more Nike sneakers changed hands in September, whether resale prices strengthened, or whether sellers earned better returns.

Those details matter since frequent trading doesn’t necessarily showcase stronger pricing power.

A coveted shoe commanding a premium tells investors something different from an oversupplied model changing hands at a discount.

September’s share also remained 4.7 percentage points below the 77.0% peak recorded in October 2023.

The improvement deserves attention, but it falls short of demonstrating that NKE has restored its former secondary-market dominance.

In short, resale transactions themselves don’t really establish an increase in the firm’s reported revenue.

Nike is deliberately accepting pain at Jordan

There is nevertheless a credible bullish interpretation – Jordan retains “consumer relevance” while Nike works to repair its distribution strategy.

On its latest earnings call, management acknowledged oversupplying iconic Jordan retro products and outlined plans to reduce the volume and frequency of selected launches.

Jordan represented 13% of NKE’s global business in Q1, while its sales declined in the mid-teens.

The investment logic is that tighter supply may eventually restore exclusivity, reduce the need for discounts, and improve the economics of future releases.

However, September’s resale share does not prove that this strategy is already succeeding.

Plus, Nike also faces a difficult trade-off: selling fewer pairs can protect a franchise’s desirability while hurting near-term revenue.

Investors buying the turnaround must accept that healthier brand positioning and faster sales growth may arrive on different schedules.

NKE shares need a strong earnings case

All in all, there’s reason to remain cautious on NKE shares; Jordan’s resale improvement is insufficient reason to load up on them today.

There sure are encouraging operating signs. Nike's performance portfolio grew at a high-single-digit rate in the first quarter, while gross margin expanded 60 basis points to 42.8%.

Yet management still projected a high-single-digit revenue decline for fiscal 2027 – underscoring how heavily the weaker businesses weigh on the recovery.

For shareholders, the decisive issue is how much “sustainable profit” Nike Inc can generate while resetting Jordan, Sportswear and Greater China; and a resale-share gain offers rather limited help in answering that valuation question.

data.title: Oil set for weekly gain as supply constraints keep prices elevated
data.description:
Oil prices held steady on Friday as uncertainty over Middle Eastern supplies continued to support the market, with no immediate resolution to the conflict in sight.

Brent crude futures traded around $105.8, while West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude stood at $97.71. Both benchmarks remained on course for weekly gains, with WTI up 6% and Brent rising roughly 1% over the week.

Reports that Washington was considering easing restrictions on some sanctioned oil tankers, alongside the International Energy Agency's (IEA) pledge to release the remaining 100 million barrels under its coordinated supply agreement, provided some support to market sentiment.

However, persistent supply concerns and escalating security risks in the Middle East continued to keep prices elevated.

US considers easing restrictions on oil tankers

Washington is reportedly considering lifting sanctions on some vessels belonging to the so-called shadow fleet, which transports oil from countries including Russia, Iran and Venezuela.

The move is aimed at easing pressure on oil transportation and curbing rising freight rates, offering a possible route to improving the flow of crude into global markets.

The IEA's planned release of the remaining 100 million barrels under its supply agreement has also helped sentiment, as governments seek to offset disruptions and improve the availability of oil.

However, these developments have done little to eliminate concerns about the durability of global supplies. Even with production and exports recovering toward pre-war levels in recent weeks, rising attacks around the region's critical shipping routes have renewed fears of further interruptions.

Strait of Hormuz remains key risk

The biggest source of pressure continues to be the Middle East, where attacks on energy infrastructure and commercial vessels are increasing transportation costs and adding to the risk premium built into oil prices.

Iran said Friday that it would reopen the Strait of Hormuz if the United States left the region. The statement comes as attacks around the vital waterway have increased over the past 10 days.

Iran has said the escalation in strikes is a response to the US blockade of its ports. The continuing confrontation has left traders uncertain about how reliably oil can move through the Gulf.

The Strait of Hormuz is a critical route for global energy shipments, and further disruption could tighten supplies and push prices higher.

The prospect of further attacks means that even barrels continuing to leave the Gulf carry an additional security premium, keeping prices elevated despite efforts to improve supply availability.

Storm loading after calm?

William Blair energy research analyst Neal Dingmann has warned that the market could face a further sharp spike in prices.

He told Yahoo Finance on Friday that major energy executives were concerned about the possibility of a so-called "super spike" if supply disruptions intensified.

Billionaire investor Paul Tudor Jones has also warned that crude prices may not have reached their peak, arguing that unresolved geopolitical risks leave room for another sharp increase.

"I'm long oil, bullish on oil. I think it can rally another $20 or $25," Jones told CNBC.

With not much headway in the Middle East conflicts, oil prices seem set to stay elevated at least in the near term.

data.title: BofA warns of risks seen in past capital cycles as concerns grow over AI boom
data.description:
Bank of America has warned that the artificial intelligence investment boom could follow a familiar pattern seen in previous capital cycles, with intensifying competition, falling prices and excess capacity potentially leaving investors disappointed despite the technology's long-term promise.

The warning comes as billions of dollars continue to flow into AI infrastructure, including data centers, advanced chips and computing capacity. The scale of investment has made AI one of the biggest bets in US industrial history, but questions are mounting over whether companies will generate sufficient returns to justify the spending.

Railways, telecommunications and the internet all created enormous economic value, but investors also lost money when capital flooded into projects whose returns failed to justify their costs.

AI-related stocks are already under pressure. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index has declined for seven consecutive sessions, leaving it around 13% below its recent high.

Bank of America analyst Sebastian Raedler has cautioned that the industry's rapid expansion could eventually undermine the profitability that initially attracted so much capital.

Bank of America flags capital cycle risks

Raedler said the AI industry could be repeating a pattern in which strong initial returns encourage companies to invest aggressively, eventually creating excess capacity and putting pressure on prices.

Expert View

“This monetization disappointment in the face of intense competition is precisely the failure mode seen in past capital cycles."

Bank of America analyst
Sebastian Raedler

“Most major capital cycles of the past have ended in disappointment, even though the underlying technology often lived up to expectations,” Raedler noted.

The concern is that a technology can transform industries and deliver substantial economic benefits without generating attractive returns for every company investing in it.

High profit margins in the early stages of an investment boom typically encourage more companies to enter the market and commit additional capital. As capacity expands and competition intensifies, businesses can lose pricing power, eroding the returns that made the investment attractive in the first place.

AI is already experiencing stronger competition at the model level, particularly from Chinese open-weight models. Average token prices have fallen around 50% since the summer, adding to concerns about whether AI developers can maintain the profitability needed to support their infrastructure spending.

Investors concerned over spending and returns

Interactive Brokers chief market analyst Steve Sosnick told Reuters that investors are increasingly questioning “the speed, the efficacy and the profitability of the rapid build-out in AI”.

Sosnick said a slowdown in data-center construction would eventually reduce demand for hardware, as customers would no longer be racing to buy equipment at almost any price.

Such a shift could affect chipmakers and other suppliers that have benefited from the surge in AI infrastructure investment. If companies scale back their construction plans, equipment purchases could weaken, particularly if falling AI prices make it more difficult to justify additional computing capacity.

As infrastructure spending continues, companies are under pressure to demonstrate that their AI products can generate enough revenue and cash flow to support the investments behind them.

Warsh offers an optimistic view

Despite the concerns over valuations and monetization, Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh struck an optimistic tone about AI's potential economic benefits on Friday.

"It's obviously hitting the demand side of the economy before it's going to hit the supply side of the economy," Warsh said.

"We don't know in the next 12 or 18 months its (AI) effect on employment, but if you believe like I believe, which is it will make economies and countries that put it to good use more productive, that it's going to make it so that we will have more wealth, then that has to be a very ​good thing."

Federal Reserve Chair
Kevin Warsh

Warsh's comments point to the potential for AI to improve productivity and generate broader economic gains as businesses adopt the technology.

However, the potential long-term benefits do not eliminate the financial risks associated with the current investment cycle.

data.title: Dow futures rise 145 points: 5 things to know before Wall Street opens on Oct. 16
data.description:
US stock futures traded mixed on Friday as Wall Street tried to end one of the year’s most volatile weeks for technology shares and Treasuries on firmer ground.

Dow futures rose about 145 points or 0.3%, S&P 500 futures gained 0.2% and Nasdaq 100 futures plunged 0.23%.

The 10-year Treasury yield held near 5.09%, well below this week’s 5.3% peak, after Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh declined to signal an October rate increase.

That eased some pressure on valuations, but AI-credit concerns remain unresolved and investors still face industrial data, regional-bank earnings and a sharp Tesla premarket move.

5 things to know before Wall Street opens

1. Warsh lowers the temperature on October rate fears

Warsh said he would not prejudge the Fed’s October 27-28 meeting, reinforcing expectations that policymakers may pause after September’s rate increase.

CME pricing put the probability of another October hike at about 15%, while The Wall Street Journal showed similar odds near 14%.

2. AI stocks stabilise, but CoreWeave keeps credit risk in focus

The AI sell-off looked calmer, but the financing problem has not disappeared.

CoreWeave fell more than 4% premarket after rebounding on Thursday, while its bonds continued to yield above 15%.

BNP Paribas analyst Daniel Wang told Barron’s that CoreWeave still has substantial revenue visibility, but said sustainable cash generation remains the key test.

AI demand is still strong; markets are questioning whether debt-funded expansion can generate adequate returns.

3. Industrial production is the next test for the bond rally

September industrial production is due at 9:15 am ET, according to the Federal Reserve.

The report matters less than CPI or PPI, but the timing is important after this week’s violent yield reversal.

Strong output could revive concern that demand remains too resilient for inflation to cool quickly, while a weak reading would strengthen the argument that borrowing costs above 5% are beginning to restrain activity.

4. Regional banks offer a cleaner read on high-rate stress

Truist Financial, M&T Bank, Citizens Financial and Regions Financial are among the lenders reporting before the bell, alongside Travelers.

Investors will focus on net interest income, deposit costs, loan growth and credit quality.

Regional banks offer a direct test of whether high rates are still supporting margins or beginning to weaken borrowers.

After this week’s bond-market swings, deterioration in deposits or credit could matter more than an earnings beat.

5. Tesla jumps after the Roadster finally returns

Tesla rose about 5% premarket after unveiling a redesigned Roadster with SpaceX-developed thrusters capable of brief aerial manoeuvres. Production is now targeted for 2028 after years of delays.

Analysts noted that the car is likely to have limited near-term financial impact, making Friday’s move more a sentiment and innovation trade than an earnings re-rating.

The test is whether enthusiasm survives once investors refocus on delivery timing and Tesla’s broader growth challenges.

data.title: Dow opens 240 pts higher as AI stocks slide and inflation concerns weigh
data.description:
US stocks opened mixed on Friday as renewed selling in technology and artificial intelligence-related stocks weighed on sentiment, while gains in Tesla offered some support.

Investors also assessed persistent inflation pressures and the outlook for Federal Reserve interest rates ahead of the central bank’s October policy meeting.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 242 points while the S&P 500 gained 0.11%. The Nasdaq composite fell 0.28%.

The S&P 500 and Nasdaq were on track for weekly losses, while the Dow remained positioned for a weekly advance.

Tesla rises as AI stocks face renewed selling

Tesla shares climbed around 0.8% in trading after the electric vehicle maker unveiled its redesigned Roadster, developed in collaboration with SpaceX and featuring rocket-style thrusters.

The vehicle is not expected to enter production until 2028.

SpaceX shares fell 2.5%.

Gains in Tesla contrasted with continued weakness across several AI-related stocks.

Nvidia-backed data centre operator CoreWeave fell 6.6% in trading, reversing some of Thursday’s rebound, as concerns about its debt burden persisted.

The company’s bonds sold off sharply this week, pushing yields above 15%.

Other neocloud companies, including Nebius Group and Iren, declined more than 5% each. Micron Technology shares fell 3.6%, while Intel dropped 2.18%.

Semiconductor stocks have also faced pressure amid concerns about growing Chinese competition in the memory chip market.

The VanEck Semiconductor ETF fell 1.7% in trading and was down 8.9% for the week.

The declines reflect investor concerns that data centre operators may struggle to generate profits quickly enough to service their debt, particularly if borrowing costs rise.

David Morrison, senior market analyst at Trade Nation, said the pullback in memory chip stocks and concerns over CoreWeave’s debt had given investors a reason to reduce exposure to companies linked to AI.

“There’s still some caution out there,” Morrison said.

"Just a touch of profit-taking after yesterday’s rebound, or something more serious? Time will tell. But it could be argued that investor behaviour since the middle of this week could provide some insight into the future.", he added.

Inflation and Fed outlook weigh on sentiment

Investors also remained focused on hotter-than-expected inflation data released this week.

US consumer and producer prices have shown persistent pressure, with wholesale inflation recording its biggest increase since 2022 and consumer inflation remaining above the Federal Reserve’s 2% target.

Elevated energy prices following the US-Iran war have added to inflation concerns, complicating the outlook for monetary policy.

Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh, speaking at an International Monetary Fund event in Bangkok, said the US economy remained resilient and was benefiting from an AI-driven investment boom.

He also noted that stronger spending was contributing to inflation, without offering a clear signal on the Fed’s next policy decision.

Markets increasingly expect the central bank to leave interest rates unchanged at its October 27-28 meeting. The CME Group’s FedWatch tool indicated an 85% probability of a hold.

Morrison also pointed to sharp movements in Treasury yields as a potential signal of changing investor sentiment.

The 10-year Treasury yield rose above 5.30% on Wednesday before falling to a three-week low on Thursday.

He said the moves could reflect concerns about a possible unwinding of the AI trade or a shift towards safer assets.

Netflix and other stocks move in trading

Among other individual stocks, Varonis Systems gained 2.7% after Thoma Bravo-owned Proofpoint agreed to acquire the data security company in an all-cash deal valued at $6.3 billion.

Netflix shares declined 1.7% after the streaming company appointed former Disney executive Peter Rice as chief content officer, replacing Bela Bajaria.

Meanwhile, concerns about AI financing costs also extended to private companies.

Reuters reported that some current and prospective investors in Anthropic’s planned initial public offering were considering a lower valuation amid worries about rising AI funding costs.

data.title: Zeta Global stock is soaring: Here is why and what comes next
data.description:
Zeta Global stock continued its strong rally, reaching its highest level since November 2024, and is slowly nearing its record high of $38.15. It has jumped by over 230% from its 2025 lows, with the market capitalization hitting $8.42 billion. This rally may continue after Goldman Sachs upgraded its target.

Goldman Sachs has upgraded Zeta Global stock target

Zeta Global is a top company in the advertising industry, where it uses artificial intelligence, customer data analytics, and digital marketing automation solutions to help clients. It works with large firms across most sectors to help them find new customers, predict what they are likely to buy, and then deliver personalized advertisements.

Goldman Sachs analysts believe that Zeta Global has more room for growth. They upgraded the company from neutral to buy, with the price target being $45, which is about 35% above the current level. The analysts pointed to its strong demand and revenues, and the need for personalized marketing. 

Other analysts have been relatively bullish on the stock. Roth Capital has set a target of $55, while New Street Research, KeyCorp, Truist Financial, and DA Davidson have a target of $38. The average target among analysts is $36, where it is trading at today.

Zeta growth to continue

The most recent financial showed that its revenue rose by 44% in the second quarter to $443 million. Its adjusted EBITDA soared by 56% to $92 million, while its adjusted EBITDA margin expanded to 20.7%.

Notably, this report was the 20th straight “beat and raise” quarter. It predicted that it is on track to hit its 2028 EBITDA and free cash flow targets. Its annual revenue is expected to jump to $2.3 billion in 2028 from $1.8 billion this year.

The adjusted EBITDA margin is expected to move to 25%. If this is correct, the figure will jump to $573 million from $405 million this year, with its free cash flow target hitting $371 million.

These numbers may help to justify its substantial valuation. It trades with a forward price-to-earnings ratio of 35, much higher than the forward S&P 500’s 19.1. 

On the positive side, the company has a forward PEG ratio of 1.04, slightly lower than the sector median of 1.17. Its Rule-of-40 multiple also stands at 100. 

Zeta Global shares technical analysis

Zeta shares chart | Source: TradingView

The weekly chart shows that Zeta Global shares have continued soaring in the past few months. It jumped from $10.6 in 2025 to a high of $35.6 as the rally gained momentum. 

The stock is in the process of forming a cup-and-handle pattern whose upper side is at $38.15, its highest point in 2024. This pattern often leads to more upside over time. 

Zeta has remained above the 50-week moving average. Therefore, the stock will likely continue rising, with the next target to watch being at $50. This view will be confirmed if it moves above the all-time high of $38.15.

data.title: XRP rebounds above $1.32 after brutal sell-off: can bulls force a $1.45 breakout?
data.description:
XRP recovered toward $1.34 after briefly dropping below $1.32 as stronger-than-expected US producer inflation unsettled cryptocurrency markets.

The token lost nearly 6% on Thursday before buyers stepped in around the closely watched support area. The rebound limited the decline, although the broader technical outlook remained bearish.

The immediate question is whether XRP can sustain its recovery above $1.32. Holding that level would signal stabilization, while another breakdown could bring $1.25 back into focus.

Hot PPI data adds to macroeconomic pressure

September’s US Producer Price Index increased 1.3% month-over-month, exceeding analyst expectations of 0.5%.

Core PPI, which excludes food and energy prices, rose 0.7% monthly against a forecast of 0.3%. That also represented an acceleration of 0.5 percentage points from the previous month.

The release followed a hotter-than-expected Consumer Price Index reading, reinforcing concerns about persistent inflation and the Federal Reserve’s policy outlook.

Although the figures initially weighed on cryptocurrencies, the subsequent recovery showed that buyers were willing to absorb supply near recent support levels.

The volatile trading followed approximately $1.7 billion in cryptocurrency liquidations over four days, according to CoinGlass.

Much of that pressure reflected a developing long squeeze, with falling prices forcing leveraged bullish positions to close.

The market’s post-PPI reversal then caught traders positioned for further losses. More than $300 million in short positions were liquidated over the last 24 hours.

Those figures cover the broader cryptocurrency market, not XRP alone. They nevertheless illustrate how sharp reversals can create losses on both sides of leveraged trading.

Demand through XRP-linked exchange-traded funds remained subdued despite the price rebound.

The products attracted approximately $13 million in net inflows so far in October, according to SoSoValue data.

The funds could record a monthly total of roughly $26 million if that pace continued, a 79% decline from September. 

Weak ETF inflows suggest these products are providing limited fresh buying support. A sustained improvement would offer stronger evidence that investment appetite is recovering alongside the token’s price.

Onchain data provides a potentially more constructive signal. According to Santiment data, XRP transfers into exchanges have declined following a pronounced increase between September 10 and September 27.

Lower exchange inflows may indicate fewer tokens are moving to trading venues for potential sale. 

However, the metric does not establish that selling has stopped or that all exchange deposits are intended for liquidation.

The decline could ease one source of supply pressure, particularly if buyers continue defending nearby support.

XRP needs $1.45 breakout to strengthen reversal case

The recovery around $1.32 keeps that area central to XRP’s near-term outlook. Sustained trading above it would support the possibility that the pullback is finding a floor. 

Further gains could also pressure remaining short positions, although a larger short squeeze would depend on positioning and follow-through buying.

The more important reversal threshold identified in the source analysis is $1.45. A sustained move above that level would strengthen the case for a change in trend.

The article’s longer-term $1.80 target remains a bullish scenario, not an immediate expectation.

Until XRP clears resistance, downside risk persists. Losing $1.32 again would weaken the rebound and increase the possibility of a retest of $1.25.

data.title: Fed rate-hold odds jump to 85% even as Warsh offers no clues on policy path
data.description:
Expectations that the Federal Reserve will hold interest rates steady at its October meeting surged on Friday, even as persistent inflation and strong economic data continued to complicate the outlook for monetary policy.

CME FedWatch data showed an 85.1% probability of the Fed leaving rates unchanged at its next meeting. That was up from around 72% a day earlier and close to an even split about a month ago.

The shift in expectations comes as investors weigh fresh inflation data against the possibility of further monetary tightening. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh, meanwhile, declined to indicate which way policymakers were leaning ahead of the upcoming decision.

The Federal Reserve raised rates by 25 basis points last month, taking its benchmark rate to a range of 3.75%-4.00%. The September move was its first rate increase in three years.

What did Warsh say?

Speaking at the International Monetary Fund and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok on Friday, Warsh maintained his stance of avoiding advance signals about the Fed's interest-rate decisions.

"I don't prejudge meetings," Warsh said during a discussion with IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva. "I don't believe in saying now what I might do at the meetings that we have in the balance of this year."

However, he reiterated the central bank's commitment to bringing inflation under control, referring to last month's rate increase as a move toward tighter monetary policy.

"We made very clear that we would deliver price stability, and we removed a dose of accommodation about a month ago."

Fed Chair
Kevin Warsh

Warsh's comments leave the October decision open, with policymakers continuing to assess incoming data as they balance inflation risks against broader economic conditions.

Inflation data complicates outlook

The Fed faces a challenging environment as price pressures remain elevated, partly because of persistently high energy costs.

Wednesday's consumer price index report showed headline inflation at 3.7% annually, while core inflation reached 2.6%. Both readings were slightly above expectations, initially raising the likelihood of another rate increase in October before those odds eased on Thursday.

The producer price index added to concerns about persistent inflation. Wholesale prices rose 1.3% in September and increased 6.3% from a year earlier, marking the largest annual increase since December 2022.

Retail sales also came in stronger than expected, advancing 0.8% against economists' consensus forecast of 0.3%.

The combination of higher producer prices and resilient consumer spending has reinforced concerns that inflation could remain difficult to contain. However, the latest figures have not prevented markets from increasingly pricing in an October pause.

December hike likely

While expectations for an October rate increase have declined, markets continue to anticipate further tightening before the end of the year.

CME FedWatch data indicated an approximately 88.9% probability of a rate increase at the Fed's December 9 meeting, up from 83% a week earlier.

UBS Global Wealth Management has also revised its forecast, expecting the Fed to extend its tightening cycle into 2027.

In a research note led by economist Andrew Dubinsky, UBS projected a quarter-point rate increase in December, followed by another 25-basis-point hike in March 2027.

The bank expects policymakers to pause after the March increase to assess the cumulative impact of higher interest rates.

data.title: US Treasury yields are still above 5%, so why have they fallen so sharply this week?
data.description:
US Treasury yields have staged a violent reversal from this week’s peak, with the 10-year pulling sharply back from 5.3% despite hotter inflation data.

The move suggests that level may be emerging as a pain threshold for the bond market.

The benchmark yield touched 5.33% after Wednesday’s CPI report, then fell to 5.086% by Thursday’s close and held near that level on Friday. Thursday’s 10-basis-point decline was its biggest one-day drop since August 2025.

That move came despite September CPI accelerating to 3.7%, producer prices jumping 6.3% year on year, stronger retail sales and oil remaining above $100.

The 5.3% Treasury level is becoming a market pain threshold

The 10-year’s reversal matters because the market has tested the 5.3% area more than once without sustaining a move higher.

Analysts noted that investors again stepped in when the yield breached 5.3% on Wednesday, pulling it back toward 5.18% before a rally in bonds on Thursday.

That does not prove 5.3% is a permanent ceiling, but suggests the level has become high enough to change investor behaviour.

Jussi Hiljanen, chief rates strategist at SEB, told Dow Jones Newswires that Treasury yields may have reached levels where “their elevated levels weigh on risk sentiment”.

The mechanism is self-limiting, as higher yields tighten financial conditions, raise mortgage and corporate borrowing costs and make equities less attractive. If those pressures begin weakening growth expectations, investors gain another reason to buy Treasuries.

That demand pushes bond prices higher and yields lower. In other words, the same rise in yields that creates the sell-off can eventually create the conditions for its reversal.

Hot inflation could not stop the Treasury rally

The more surprising part is what the bond market chose to ignore.

Wednesday’s CPI report showed headline inflation at 3.7% and core inflation at 2.6%, slightly above expectations.

Thursday then brought an even stronger shock, as producer prices rose 1.3% in September and 6.3% from a year earlier, the largest annual increase since December 2022. Retail sales also gained 0.8%, far above the 0.3% consensus.

Yet Treasury yields continued falling.

Prashant Newnaha, senior rates strategist at TD Securities, told Reuters the bond rally after hot CPI was “highly counter-intuitive”.

His explanation was that the AI sell-off was forcing markets to mark down growth expectations, allowing bonds to reclaim their role as a hedge against falling stocks.

That shift matters because Treasuries had offered little protection during much of 2026. Inflation fears, heavy issuance and rising oil prices often pushed bond yields higher at the same time equities were under pressure.

But this week, investors increasingly treated high yields themselves as part of the risk, particularly as heavily leveraged AI infrastructure companies faced surging financing costs.

The bond-market peak is still far from certain

Declaring 5.3% the final top would still be premature, as inflation remains well above the Federal Reserve’s target, oil prices are elevated and policymakers may not be finished tightening.

After Wednesday’s CPI report, futures briefly priced roughly even odds of an October rate increase. Thursday’s data later pushed those odds lower, but the debate remains open.

PIMCO chief investment officer Daniel Ivascyn told Reuters this week that Treasury yields may not have peaked and that the Fed could still raise rates once or twice more.

That is the central counterargument to the pain-threshold thesis.

A 5.3% yield can attract buyers while still failing to cap the market permanently if inflation remains sticky, federal borrowing stays heavy or the Fed turns more hawkish.

The latest move should therefore be viewed as a violent reversal from the week’s peak, not proof that the bond sell-off is over.
